text.p: These are some of the main stories in Sofia newspapers today. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- Bulgaria's cabinet has too many responsibilities and can not add to them the responsibility for the lev/dollar exchange rate, which lies with the central bank, deputy prime minister Roumen Gechev told reporters after the lev nosedived to 395 per dollar on Thursday, losing 18 percent to the dollar on the day.
-- Only 0.3 percent of Bulgarians are optimistic about the country's economic prospects while 80 percent think prices will keep rising, a National Statistics Institute (NSI) poll showed.
-- Bulgaria's Transport Minister Stamen Stamenov agreed with his Roumanian counterpart in Sofia to renew bilateral negotiations for the setting of a new bridge over the Danube river.
-- An official from the Bulgarian private Security Insurance Company and his bodyguard were killed by a bomb planted in an appartment elevator in the Black sea port of Varna, local police said.
-- Bulgaria's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is expected to fall by 10 percent this year, topping the previous record high fall of 9.2 percent in 1991, the NSI said.
-- Bulgaria's state industrial output fell by 6.5 percent in October against the same month last year, and the private industrial output fell by 10 percent for the same period, NSI figures showed.

-- Bulgaria's ministries of agriculture, industry, transport, construction and trade posted six billion levs in sell-off proceeds from the beginning of the year until November 15, government data showed.

-- Bulgaria's Post and Telecommunication Committee (PTC) proposed to the cabinet to raise prices of phone calls by 40 percent from December due to the rapid fall of the Bulgarian lev against the dollar, PTC chairman Lyubomir Kolarov said.
-- Bulgaria's State Railways (BSR) will raise cargo tariffs by 30 percent from December, bringing the cumulative rise for the year to 56 percent, BSR general director Angel Dimitrov said.

-- Bulgaria is on the verge of hyperinflation and it is necessary to negotiate rescheduling of debt payments to the Paris club of government creditors, which total $500 million for 1997, Trade Minister Atanas Paparizov said.
